91/1,000 candidates never downloaded (exhausted retries within the run's time budget -- treated as permanent, not chased further, per the 4-hour stage cap). Feature-extraction yield (16.7%) matches the pilot's observed rate (18.5% at n=275) within normal variation -- most attrition here is single-sector light curves lacking enough transits for multi-transit-dependent features (FAP, odd-even mismatch, transit shape), not a bug.

These are unexamined candidates ranked for human review -- not confirmed detections, not discoveries. A high score means "worth a closer look by someone qualified to vet it," not "this is a planet." Real confirmation requires spectroscopic follow-up, multiple independent observations, and ruling out instrumental/astrophysical false-positive scenarios this light-curve-only model cannot see.

Deep verification & physical characterization

A follow-up automated stage re-checked every trustworthy candidate against four external sources live -- ExoFOP-TESS, the NASA Exoplanet Archive, AAVSO's Variable Star Index (VSX) via Vizier, and Gaia DR3 -- then derived real physical parameters (planet radius, orbital distance, equilibrium temperature) from the transit fit and stellar parameters already in hand.

Last verified unknown as of 2026-07-15 01:12:40 UTC -- the NASA Exoplanet Archive (confirmed planets + full TOI table) and the ExoFOP-TESS bulk CSV were both re-queried live immediately before this report was generated, not reused from the original run. Result: identical counts (4,450 confirmed-planet TICs, 7,753 TOI TICs) and zero of the 105 candidates have been claimed by anyone since -- confirmed unchanged, not assumed. The already-known check was additionally validated against a real confirmed-planet host (Kepler-1597, TIC 158722002), not just fake IDs, to make sure it actually catches a true positive.

Three real bugs were caught and fixed in this consolidation pass, on top of the one below:
  1. Blind Gaia-first-row assumption. The blending check assumed the closest Gaia cone-search result was always the target star itself. For faint red stars Gaia's astrometric solution sometimes doesn't return the target at all -- silently treating a real nearby neighbor as "the star" and discarding it as blend risk. Fixed to verify separation <2" before assuming it's the target; otherwise the risk is now honestly reported as UNKNOWN rather than silently as low.
  2. Magnitude-blind blend categorization. A neighbor 21-63" away was automatically labeled high/moderate risk regardless of brightness. A source 6+ magnitudes fainter than the target contributes negligible dilution no matter how close. Fixed with a brightness-aware "LOW-MODERATE" tier -- this alone is why high-blend count dropped from 81 to 32 between runs.
  3. Ambiguous status-string aggregation. Summary counts used substring checks like "no match" that would have silently miscounted a network error as a hit. Every external check now returns an explicit HIT/NO_HIT/ERROR/SKIPPED code instead.
A bug was caught and fixed mid-run: the first pass at checking ExoFOP for "already flagged" activity had a 100% false-positive rate -- ExoFOP's per-target page renders the same templated structure for literally any TIC ID, including a deliberately fake one that doesn't exist. Confirmed by testing a fake TIC and two random, definitely- unflagged stars from this project's own pool before trusting the result. Fixed to check for an actual TOI-#### designation string instead, which correctly distinguishes real activity (verified against TOI-6293) from the templated shell. All numbers below reflect the corrected check.

ADS literature search was skipped -- the API returned HTTP 401 without an authorization token; it needs a free API key (an ADS account + a generated token at ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/user/settings/token) that isn't available in this environment. The free arXiv API was used as a partial substitute (preprints only, not the full ADS index) -- 0 hits among the 105.

The honest physical-parameter picture is sobering. Median derived planet radius across the 105 is 8.8 Earth radii (mean 33, max 336) -- far too large for most of these to plausibly be real planets; combined with 97% (102/105) having a Gaia-catalogued source within 3 TESS pixels and 36% matching a known variable star, the more likely explanation for most of this list is blended eclipsing binaries or contaminated photometry, not planets. This doesn't contradict the earlier out-of-distribution work -- it's a different, complementary failure mode those checks weren't designed to catch (implausible transit-derived physical size, not an implausible feature vector).
A fourth bug was found while implementing the stellar-mass badge below: the TIC catalog's stellar mass was fetched and even used to run the actual transit-fit (it affects the duration model), but was silently dropped when the final candidate table got assembled -- every candidate showed a "missing mass" regardless of what TIC actually had on file, incorrectly implying 105/105 relied on a solar-mass default. Fixed the merge and recomputed every physical parameter from scratch; the real number is 41/105 genuinely defaulted -- the rest used their actual catalog mass all along.
Correction from the previous version of this report: TIC_120442975 was previously singled out as the standout candidate (plausible 2.0 R⊕ planet, 303K, "only a faint distant neighbor"). Under the corrected blending check, Gaia's astrometric solution never actually matched this target star at all -- the nearest returned source, at 2.3" and G=15.4, may well be a fainter-than-thought neighbor, or may be the star itself misresolved. Either way, its blend risk is honestly UNKNOWN, not low, and it no longer clears the combined filter below. It also has only 6 transits at a marginal SDE of 6.2. Its stellar mass, now that the bug above is fixed, turns out to be a real TIC catalog value after all -- the corrected equilibrium temperature is 401K, not the 303K reported before (which used an incorrectly-defaulted solar mass). 401K is well outside the rough habitable-zone band. Two independent reasons for doubt remain (unresolved blend risk, marginal transit count), and the earlier "inside the habitable zone" framing was wrong on top of being premature. It remains an interesting, unflagged candidate, but "closer look" should mean a manual Gaia image inspection first, not a habitable-zone headline.
Web-app follow-up evidence for the top-ranked candidate, TIC_403153811 (added since this CSV-based report was first generated): two on-demand automated checks were run and verified against real data. Multi-sector strengthening combined all 3 available sectors (102, 103, 104) into one longer baseline and re-ran the transit search: the signal holds up -- 548 ppm depth (consistent with the single-sector value), SDE improved to 12.5 (from 7.2), 93 transits observed in total. This is supplementary evidence only; it is not fed back through the classifier or OOD checks. Pixel-level centroid check: the transit signal's photocenter is shifted 1.53 pixels from the target's catalog position -- corroborating, independently, the "moderate" Gaia blend-risk flag already on this candidate. Neither check moves this candidate to "confirmed" -- both are additional reasons for informed follow-up, not a substitute for it.

Combined-filter ranking (the real "best candidates" list)

This is now the default, permanent ranking method for every future run of this pipeline -- not a one-off analysis of this batch. It combines classifier probability with passing both out-of-distribution checks, a physically plausible derived radius (<2 Jupiter radii -- see reasoning below), no known variable-star match, and moderate-or- better Gaia blend risk. Of 105 candidates, 26 survive this combined filter; 0 survive the stricter low-blend- only tier. None reach the "High" confidence tier -- the best of them reach "Medium." Physical plausibility ceiling: 2 Jupiter radii (22.4 R⊕). The largest confirmed transiting exoplanets (inflated hot Jupiters) top out near this size, and giant planets/brown dwarfs occupy a narrow radius band regardless of mass, due to electron-degeneracy pressure -- anything meaningfully larger derived from a transit fit is almost certainly a blended eclipsing binary (a small star), not a planet. 36/105 candidates exceed this ceiling.

Every candidate's stellar mass provenance is now surfaced explicitly: 41/105 had no real mass in the TIC catalog and fell back to a solar-mass assumption, which degrades the reliability of their semi-major-axis/equilibrium-temperature/insolation estimates -- worth weighting accordingly when comparing candidates on those fields.

Needs manual review (2 candidates)

Separate from the combined filter and from exclusion: these candidates clear every other bar (unflagged, no VSX match, physically plausible radius) but Gaia's astrometric solution never resolved the target star itself, so blend risk is honestly UNKNOWN -- not verified low, but also not verified high. Automatically excluding these would discard exactly the kind of candidate that deserves a human glance at a Gaia finder-chart image before anything else.

What was skipped

91/1,000 candidates never downloaded within the run's time budget (retries exhausted -- treated as permanent per the established cache-clear-then-accept pattern from earlier pilots). 767 downloaded stars did not yield a complete feature set (mostly single-sector baselines too short for multi-transit features) -- expected, not a bug. 35 scored candidates were flagged out-of-distribution (see the full ranked_candidates_out_of_distribution.csv) and are not included above -- they may be interesting but the model has no learned behavior for feature values that extreme.

Autonomous decision log (every choice made without stopping to ask)
10:43:57Starting Part 1: single-sector approach, sample-size 1,000, top-n 50. Multi-sector approach explicitly rejected per the prior pilot finding (78% OOD-flag rate vs ~20% for single-sector -- the model wasn't trained to handle multi-sector's longer periods/higher transit counts).
12:53:26Full pipeline completed successfully on attempt 6 of the retry loop (stage elapsed 1,100s of a 4-hour budget). Total elapsed at Part 1 completion: 7,769s (~2h 9m) of the 9-hour overall budget.
13:22:00Starting Part 2: independent Gaia/SIMBAD stellar-parameter verification for the 105 trustworthy candidates. Scope determination logged in 07_search_unknown.py's docstring: the original placeholder scripts 07 (search) and 08 (rank) are fully redundant with what 06 already does (download, preprocess, TLS, score, rank, both OOD checks, explanations, plots) -- not rebuilt. The one genuine remaining gap was that every stellar parameter used both as a model feature and as the OOD check's basis came from a single source (TIC catalog), never independently verified -- closed via Gaia DR3 + SIMBAD cross-checks.
13:27:03Part 2 completed successfully on attempt 1. Neither retry loop needed its budget cap or truncation fallback -- both stages finished cleanly within normal operating time.
Known environment quirk handled automatically throughout

This environment intermittently raises a spurious "I/O operation on closed file" error tied to a leftover background thread racing the main process's console output -- confirmed harmless to the underlying data (every stage checkpoints to disk independently of console output) across dozens of occurrences this session. Both pipeline stages were wrapped in an automatic retry loop that re-invokes the script on this specific error and otherwise leaves any other error to surface normally. No manual intervention was needed during this run.
